title: Lists and tuples
summary: Build a to-do list you can change with append, remove and sort, and see why a tuple refuses to change.
objectives: Add, remove and sort items in a list
Explain that a tuple is immutable (it cannot be changed)
Catch an error with try and except and print a friendly message

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

A list is a collection you can change: you can add items, take them out and sort them. A tuple looks similar but is immutable, which means that once it is made, nothing inside it can be changed. In this lab you build a small task tracker with a list: add a task, remove a finished one, sort the rest and print the final list. Then you take a tuple holding an RGB colour, try to change one of its numbers, and catch the `TypeError` Python raises so your program can explain it in a friendly message instead of crashing.

segments.title: Lab: task tracker and a fixed colour

lab.title: Task tracker and a fixed colour
lab.objective: Change a list with append, remove and sort, then show that a tuple cannot be changed by catching the TypeError.
lab.instructions:
Part 1: the task tracker. The list tasks starts with three tasks.

1. Add "walk the dog" to the end with .append().
2. Remove "buy milk" with .remove().
3. Sort the list into alphabetical order with .sort().
4. Print the list. It should show ['call grandma', 'do homework', 'walk the dog'].

Part 2: the fixed colour. The tuple colour holds an RGB colour (0, 128, 255).

5. Inside a try block, try to change the first number: colour[0] = 255. Python refuses and raises a TypeError.
6. In an except TypeError block, print a friendly one-line message that contains the word TypeError, for example: TypeError: a tuple cannot be changed.
7. Print colour to show it is unchanged.
lab.constraints: Keep the variable names tasks and colour. Use the list methods .append(), .remove() and .sort(); do not retype the list. Keep colour as the tuple (0, 128, 255). Do not use input().
lab.starter_code:
# Part 1: a task tracker built on a list
tasks = ["do homework", "buy milk", "call grandma"]

# 1. Add "walk the dog" to the end of the list with .append()

# 2. Remove "buy milk" with .remove()

# 3. Sort the list with .sort()

# 4. Print the final list
print(tasks)

# Part 2: a tuple that cannot be changed
colour = (0, 128, 255)

# 5. Inside a try block, try to change the first value: colour[0] = 255
# 6. In an except TypeError block, print a friendly message
#    that contains the word TypeError

# 7. Print colour to show it did not change
print(colour)
hints: List methods change the list in place: tasks.append("walk the dog") adds to the end, tasks.remove("buy milk") takes that item out, tasks.sort() puts the items in order. Each goes on its own line, before print(tasks).

A try block runs code that might fail; the except block runs only when that error happens. Write try: then colour[0] = 255 indented underneath, then except TypeError: and an indented print under that.
Inside except TypeError: write print("TypeError: a tuple cannot be changed"). After the whole try/except, print(colour) shows it is still (0, 128, 255).

lab.solution:
tasks = ["do homework", "buy milk", "call grandma"]

tasks.append("walk the dog")
tasks.remove("buy milk")
tasks.sort()
print(tasks)

colour = (0, 128, 255)

try:
    colour[0] = 255
except TypeError:
    print("TypeError: a tuple cannot be changed")

print(colour)
